newsitem.title: UK: British civil servants face Gulf War illness probe.
newsitem.headline: British civil servants face Gulf War illness probe.

text.p: British Defence Ministry staff face disciplinary action after parliament was misled about the use of pesticides blamed for causing crippling illnesses in Gulf War veterans, a minister said on Wednesday.

Nicholas Soames, minister for the armed forces, told parliament's Defence Committee he had given incorrect answers to parliamentary questions on the use of organophosphates in the Gulf in 1991 after receiving "flawed and inaccurate advice".
"The appropriate...authorities have decided that the conduct of a number of service officers and civil servants warrants further investigation," Soames told the committee.
But the opposition Labour Party demanded Soames's resignation, accusing him of "disgraceful and dishonourable" handling of the issue.
Soames in December admitted for the first time that pesticides had been more widely used in the Gulf War than admitted and apologised to parliament.
He said the government would pay compensation to sick veterans if negligence was proved and announced a new research programme.

Richard Mottram, the defence ministry's senior civil servant, told the committee on Wednesday: "There is the prospect of proceedings (against military officers) which are effectively analogous to criminal proceedings."

Lawyers representing more than 1,000 British veterans say a cocktail of immunisations to protect them against chemical and biological warfare and to help them adjust to desert conditions is the likely cause of Gulf War Syndrome.
Sufferers, some of whom are now in wheelchairs and say their children have suffered birth defects, have reported chronic fatigue, asthma and skin complaints.

One sufferer, Richard Turnbull, who helped build air force bunkers during the war in which U.S., British and other troops evicted Iraqi troops from Kuwait, told BBC radio he used a high volume smoke machine to kill animals such as scorpions.

Although the machine used organophosphates, he was not given protective clothing or a mask. Now he is suffering from emphysema, angina, hardening of the arteries and athritis and has been told he will never work again.
Soames said on Wednesday there were indications in 1995 that these chemicals had been used, but "these were not properly assessed or followed up."
Last June, when it became known for certain that organophosphates were used, the department was slow in setting the record straight, Soames said.
"I very much regret that the original mistake occurred and that it took so long to deal with it," he said.
Government sources said there had been no effort by ministers to cover up the problem of Gulf War Syndrome.
But Labour defence spokesman David Clark said Soames had no alternative but to resign immediately.
"He is fiddling while Gulf War veterans suffer. This is disgraceful and dishonourable. He is simply trying to pass the buck on to civil servants," he said.
